beats.narration: Begin by framing Course Foundations & Prerequisites as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-471. Consider this worked case: A senior computer science major who has not yet taken CSCI-471 can enroll in this course to explore historical and current perspectives. On screen, display a course eligibility matrix highlighting the fourth-year requirement and the CSCI-471 exclusion rule. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

beats.narration: Now define Early History of Computer Science precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Topics include an early history of Computer Science, a study of the people who shaped Computer Science, and a discussion of major milestones in Computer Science. Consider this worked case: Ancient Babylonian and Greek mathematical methods laid the groundwork for later algorithmic thinking in computing. On screen, show a timeline graphic connecting ancient mathematical practices to the development of modern algorithms. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Early History of Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a timeline graphic connecting ancient mathematical practices to the development of modern algorithms.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how People Who Shaped Computer Science operates in a concrete sequence. Students who have a background in Computer Science theories, algorithms, and data structures will be provided a look at the history of Computer Science from historical and current perspectives. Consider this worked case: Historical figures like Ada Lovelace and Alan Turing are recognized for their foundational work in programming and theoretical computation. On screen, present a portrait collage of key historical figures with brief annotations on their specific contributions. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: People Who Shaped Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Present a portrait collage of key historical figures with brief annotations on their specific contributions.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Major Milestones in Computer Science and make the decision criteria explicit. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Consider this worked case: The invention of the transistor and the development of integrated circuits marked pivotal shifts in hardware architecture and processing power. On screen, display a slide sequence showing key hardware and software milestones with dates and brief impact statements. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Major Milestones in Computer Science
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a slide sequence showing key hardware and software milestones with dates and brief impact statements.

beats.narration: Apply Secure Software Development Framework to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Consider this worked case: Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development, ensuring foundational readiness before coding begins. On screen, show a four-quadrant diagram mapping each practice group to its core responsibilities and deliverables. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Secure Software Development Framework
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a four-quadrant diagram mapping each practice group to its core responsibilities and deliverables.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Cryptographic Standards & Confidentiality, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Consider this worked case: AES encryption standards specify block sizes and key lengths that ensure data remains unreadable without proper authentication. On screen, display a comparison table of AES modes of operation showing how each processes data larger than one block. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Cryptographic Standards & Confidentiality
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a comparison table of AES modes of operation showing how each processes data larger than one block.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Integrity, Authenticity & Key Management with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Consider this worked case: Digital signatures verify the origin of a message, and key rotation policies ensure compromised keys are replaced before expiration. On screen, illustrate a key lifecycle flowchart showing generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, and destruction steps. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Integrity, Authenticity & Key Management
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a key lifecycle flowchart showing generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, and destruction steps.

beats.narration: Use Verification & Security Reasoning to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities. Consider this worked case: Security reasoning maps a web application's trust boundaries to identify where user input enters the system and where data is stored. On screen, show a trust boundary diagram highlighting assets, threats, and controls within a software architecture. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Verification & Security Reasoning
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a trust boundary diagram highlighting assets, threats, and controls within a software architecture.

beats.narration: Connect Current Issues: Legal, Ethical & Privacy to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. Additionally, students will study current issues in Computer Science, including legal, ethical, diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility and privacy issues, and how past issues affect modern designs and decision making by computer scientists. Consider this worked case: Privacy regulations like GDPR require data minimization and user consent mechanisms in modern application design. On screen, display a checklist of current CS issues with icons representing legal, ethical, DEI, accessibility, and privacy domains. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Current Issues: Legal, Ethical & Privacy
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a checklist of current CS issues with icons representing legal, ethical, DEI, accessibility, and privacy domains.

beats.narration: Finish with Past Issues Affecting Modern Design as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Consider this worked case: Early vulnerabilities in cryptographic protocols led to modern side-channel attack mitigations and stricter validation checks in implementations. On screen, show a cause-and-effect diagram linking historical security failures to contemporary design standards and validation practices. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Past Issues Affecting Modern Design
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a cause-and-effect diagram linking historical security failures to contemporary design standards and validation practices.

sources.excerpt: The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.
sources.title: NIST Secure Software Development Framework

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.
sources.title: NIST Cryptographic Standards and Guidelines
